title: Lab Safety Quiz
subtitle: 20 Questions · Multiple Choice & True/False · Full Answer Key with Explanations

items: Read each question carefully and choose the best answer.
Write your answer letter in the blank provided.
No calculators needed — this quiz checks safety knowledge, not math.

items.q: Which symbol warns that a chemical is corrosive?
items.answer: Corrosion (hand and surface)
items.explain: The corrosion symbol shows a hand and a surface being eaten away — it means the chemical can burn skin and damage materials.

items.q: What should you do FIRST if a chemical splashes into your eyes?
choices: Tell the teacher and rinse eyes at the eyewash station for 15 minutes
items.answer: Tell the teacher and rinse eyes at the eyewash station for 15 minutes
items.explain: Immediate, prolonged rinsing (15 min) at the eyewash station is the correct response; tell the teacher so they can help.

items.q: Why must you never taste chemicals in the lab?
choices: They may be poisonous or corrosive
It is not hygienic to share
items.answer: They may be poisonous or corrosive
items.explain: Lab chemicals are not food-grade; many are toxic, corrosive, or carcinogenic. Never taste, smell directly, or touch chemicals.

items.q: Which glassware is safest to heat a liquid in?
choices: A beaker made of borosilicate glass
items.answer: A beaker made of borosilicate glass
items.explain: Borosilicate glass (Pyrex) resists thermal shock; graduated cylinders and plastic are not for heating.

items.q: What does the flame symbol on a container indicate?
choices: The chemical is a strong oxidizer
The chemical is explosive when wet
items.answer: The chemical is flammable
items.explain: The flame symbol (or flame-over-circle for oxidizers) means the substance can catch fire easily.

items.q: When diluting concentrated sulfuric acid, you should:
choices: Add water to the acid quickly
Add acid to water slowly while stirring
Mix them in a closed container
items.answer: Add acid to water slowly while stirring
items.explain: Dilution of acid releases heat; adding acid to water slowly lets the heat dissipate safely (AAA: Add Acid to water).

items.q: What is the correct way to smell a chemical in the lab?
choices: Put your nose directly over the container
Waft: wave the vapors toward your nose
Smell it only if it is labeled safe
items.answer: Waft: wave the vapors toward your nose
items.explain: Wafting (wafting vapors toward the nose with your hand) minimizes exposure to potentially harmful vapors.

items.q: Long hair in the lab should be:
items.answer: Tied back
items.explain: Loose hair can catch fire or dip into chemicals; tie it back and away from flames.

items.q: Which of these is an example of safe lab behavior?
choices: Wearing safety goggles and closed-toe shoes
items.answer: Wearing safety goggles and closed-toe shoes
items.explain: Goggles protect eyes; closed-toe shoes protect feet. Food, open sandals, and phones are hazards.

items.q: If you break a piece of glassware, you should:
choices: Pick up the pieces with your bare hands
Leave it and tell the teacher
Sweep it up carefully and tell the teacher
items.answer: Sweep it up carefully and tell the teacher
items.explain: Broken glass must be swept (never picked up bare-handed) and disposed of in the glass disposal container; always inform the teacher.

items.q: The GHS exclamation mark symbol indicates:
items.answer: A health hazard or irritant
items.explain: The exclamation mark warns of moderate hazards: skin/eye irritation, respiratory irritation, or other health effects.

items.q: What should you do with leftover chemicals at the end of the lab?
choices: Return them to the original bottle
items.answer: Follow your teacher's disposal instructions
items.explain: Never pour chemicals down the sink or return them to stock bottles — contamination is dangerous. Use the designated waste container.

items.q: Why is it important to read the label BEFORE using a chemical?
choices: To know the hazards and handling instructions
items.answer: To know the hazards and handling instructions
items.explain: The label (including GHS pictograms and hazard statements) tells you what the chemical is and how to handle it safely.

items.q: In case of a small fire on the lab bench, the first action is to:
choices: Use the fire extinguisher immediately without warning anyone
Notify the teacher and use the appropriate extinguisher or fire blanket
items.answer: Notify the teacher and use the appropriate extinguisher or fire blanket
items.explain: Small fires are best handled calmly with the right extinguisher/blanket; always alert the teacher first.

items.q: The skull-and-crossbones symbol means the chemical is:
choices: Acutely toxic — can cause serious harm or death if swallowed or inhaled
items.answer: Acutely toxic — can cause serious harm or death if swallowed or inhaled
items.explain: The skull warns of acute toxicity: even small amounts can be fatal if ingested, inhaled, or absorbed.

items.q: It is acceptable to work alone in the lab during free period.
items.answer: False
items.explain: Lab work requires teacher supervision; working alone is unsafe because no one can help in an emergency.

items.q: Safety goggles should be worn even when doing a 'quick' procedure.
items.answer: True
items.explain: Most lab injuries happen during quick, routine steps — wear goggles the entire time you are in the lab.

items.q: If a chemical gets on your skin, you should tell the teacher immediately and rinse the area with water.
items.answer: True
items.explain: Immediate rinsing (flushing) with water for at least 15 minutes and telling the teacher is the standard first aid.

items.q: You can use a bunsen burner near paper towels as long as you are careful.
items.answer: False
items.explain: Flammable materials (paper, cloth) must be kept away from open flames; 'being careful' is not enough.

items.q: All accidents, even minor ones, should be reported to the teacher.
items.answer: True
items.explain: Reporting even small spills or cuts lets the teacher prevent bigger problems and document what happened.
